title: How a Pair of White Sneakers Makes Emily Blunt the Perfect Sci-Fi Heroine
summary: Margaret Fairchild knows what her clothes say about her. As a Kansas City broadcast meteorologist, she's on air every morning in brightly colored body-con dresses, full glam, and high heels—the expected uniform. But when she leaves the house, she's wearing plain white sneakers. They're practical for commuting, keep her heels pristine, and, as Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day unfolds, become a quiet symbol of who she really is. Costume designer Paul Tazewell, an Oscar winner for Wicked, makes those sneakers unmissable. They're on Margaret's feet when we first meet her, when she has an on-air freakout that lands her in the hospital, and when a friendly cardinal unlocks latent communication powers—suddenly she's speaking fluent Russian and reading minds. Most crucially, they're on her feet when she realizes the suits outside her hospital room aren't the FBI. She throws on jeans, a sweater, and those sneakers and gets the hell out of there. The footwear choice is a deliberate character beat. Screenwriter David Koepp and Spielberg want us to see Margaret as steady, practical, and relatable—someone who can stand on her own two feet, comfortably. In a genre where female characters are often hobbled by ridiculous heels (the Jurassic World Bryce Dallas Howard debacle still stings), this feels like a quiet revolution. Tazewell's sneakers don't just serve the plot; they tell us everything about the kind of heroine Margaret is. She's normal enough to believe in when aliens invade and a train chase erupts, yet extraordinary enough to change the course of human history. The shoes ground her, literally and figuratively, making her the perfect anchor for Spielberg's spectacle. Sometimes the most powerful costume choice is the one that lets a woman run.
why_it_matters: The sneakers show that being sensible doesn't make a character boring—it can be a quiet act of rebellion against outdated movie clichés. It reminds viewers that heroes can be ordinary people, and that practical choices can be powerful statements about who we are.

background_read: Steven Spielberg, one of cinema's most famous directors, has made many sci-fi films like E.T. and Close Encounters, and his new project features an ordinary meteorologist as the unlikely hero.

The 'high-heels problem' became notorious in the 2015 film Jurassic World, where actress Bryce Dallas Howard's character fled dinosaurs in impractical stilettos, drawing criticism for unrealistic and sexist costuming.
Paul Tazewell, the costume designer for this film, is a Tony and Oscar-winning artist (he won an Oscar for Wicked in 2024) known for using clothing to reveal character psychology.

In recent years, filmmakers have increasingly prioritized practical footwear for female leads, as seen in movies like Mad Max: Fury Road and others, signaling a shift toward more believable, relatable heroines.
The white sneakers in this story also tie into everyday fashion trends where functional sneakers symbolize a rejection of discomfort and a focus on authenticity.

perspectives.description: The sneakers empower a female lead by prioritizing comfort and agency, breaking away from sexualized costume tropes. It makes the character more believable and relatable to audiences, showing that a heroine's strength doesn't need to come at the cost of practicality.

Some might argue that such a small detail is overhyped as a 'revolution.' True gender equity in film requires bigger structural changes—in writing, directing, and production—than a pair of shoes. Focusing on footwear alone can distract from deeper inequalities.

The choice reflects a broader cultural shift toward athleisure and functional fashion in everyday life. In film, costumes increasingly signal character psychology rather than just aesthetics, and the sneakers fit a trend where mundane objects ground extraordinary stories.

This could encourage more filmmakers to ground sci-fi heroes in realistic, everyday details, making extraordinary stories feel closer to home. It may inspire future productions to think carefully about how costuming shapes audience connection and the types of heroes we celebrate.
